description: Environmental Science & Ecology question bank derived from the provided study guide. Covers Ecology, Natural Resources, Biodiversity, Pollution & Waste, Climate & Global Issues, Environmental Protection in India, and exam cautions. No duplicate questions.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What is ecology?

options.A: Study of rocks and minerals
options.B: Scientific study of interactions among organisms and their environment

questions.explanation: Ecology is the scientific study of interactions among organisms and between organisms and their physical, chemical and biological environment.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: Who coined the term 'ecology'?

options.A: Charles Darwin
options.B: Ernst Haeckel

questions.explanation: Ernst Haeckel, a German biologist, introduced the term 'Okologie' in 1866.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: In which year was the term 'ecology' introduced?
questions.explanation: Ernst Haeckel introduced the term 'Okologie' in 1866.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What is the scope of ecology?

options.A: Only organisms and populations
options.B: Organisms, populations, communities, ecosystems, biomes, biosphere, energy flow, nutrient cycling, biodiversity and human impacts

questions.explanation: Ecology's scope includes organisms, populations, communities, ecosystems, biomes, the biosphere, energy flow, nutrient cycling, biodiversity and human impacts on nature.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What is an ecosystem?

options.A: Only living organisms in an area
options.B: A functional unit of nature where living organisms interact with one another and with non-living components
options.C: Only non-living components of an area

questions.explanation: An ecosystem is a functional unit of nature in which living organisms interact with one another and with non-living components of their surroundings.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What are the two broad components of an ecosystem?

options.A: Producers and consumers
options.B: Biotic and abiotic components

questions.explanation: The two broad components are biotic components (living organisms) and abiotic components (non-living physical and chemical factors).

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: Which of the following is an abiotic component of an ecosystem?

options.A: Green plants
options.B: Bacteria

questions.explanation: Abiotic components include non-living factors such as sunlight, temperature, water, air, soil, minerals, pH, salinity and humidity.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: Biotic components of an ecosystem are commonly grouped as:

options.A: Producers, consumers and decomposers
options.B: Herbivores, carnivores and omnivores only

questions.explanation: Biotic components are living components, commonly grouped as producers, consumers and decomposers.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What are producers in an ecosystem?

options.A: Organisms that feed on other organisms
options.B: Autotrophs that manufacture organic food from inorganic substances, usually through photosynthesis
options.C: Organisms that break down dead matter
options.D: Organisms that feed on primary consumers

questions.explanation: Producers are autotrophs that manufacture organic food from inorganic substances, usually through photosynthesis; green plants, algae and some bacteria are examples.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What are consumers in an ecosystem?

options.A: Organisms that manufacture their own food
options.B: Organisms that obtain energy by feeding on other organisms or organic matter
options.C: Organisms that break down dead matter only

questions.explanation: Consumers obtain energy by feeding on other organisms or organic matter; they include herbivores, carnivores and omnivores.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What are primary consumers?

options.A: Organisms that feed on secondary consumers
options.B: Organisms that feed directly on producers; commonly herbivores
options.C: Organisms that break down dead matter
options.D: Organisms that manufacture their own food

questions.explanation: Primary consumers feed directly on producers; they are commonly herbivores such as deer, rabbits and grasshoppers.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What are secondary consumers?

options.A: Organisms that feed on producers
options.B: Organisms that feed on primary consumers; may be carnivores or omnivores
options.C: Organisms that break down dead matter
options.D: Organisms that manufacture their own food

questions.explanation: Secondary consumers feed on primary consumers; they may be carnivores or omnivores.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What are tertiary consumers?

options.A: Organisms that feed on producers
options.B: Organisms that feed on primary consumers
options.C: Consumers that feed on secondary consumers; often occupy higher trophic positions
options.D: Organisms that break down dead matter

questions.explanation: Tertiary consumers feed on secondary consumers and often occupy higher trophic positions in a food chain.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What are decomposers?

options.A: Organisms that manufacture their own food
options.B: Organisms that feed on primary consumers
options.C: Organisms, especially bacteria and fungi, that break down dead organic matter and wastes into simpler substances
options.D: Organisms that feed on secondary consumers

questions.explanation: Decomposers, especially bacteria and fungi, break down dead organic matter and wastes into simpler substances, returning nutrients to the environment.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What is a detritivore?

options.A: An organism that manufactures its own food
options.B: An organism that ingests dead organic matter or detritus, such as earthworms and many millipedes
options.C: An organism that feeds only on living plants

questions.explanation: A detritivore ingests dead organic matter or detritus, such as earthworms and many millipedes; detritivores differ from microbial decomposers.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What is a food chain?

options.A: A network of interconnected food chains
options.B: A linear sequence showing transfer of food and energy from one organism to another, beginning with a producer or detritus
options.C: A graphical representation of trophic levels
options.D: A group of individuals of the same species

questions.explanation: A food chain is a linear sequence showing transfer of food and energy from one organism to another, beginning with a producer or detritus.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: Which of the following is an example of a grazing food chain?

options.A: Grass → grasshopper → frog → snake → eagle
options.B: Dead leaves → earthworm → bird

questions.explanation: Grass → grasshopper → frog → snake → eagle is a grazing food chain; the exact chain varies by ecosystem.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What is a food web?

options.A: A single linear sequence of energy transfer
options.B: A network of interconnected food chains representing multiple feeding relationships

questions.explanation: A food web is a network of interconnected food chains that represents the multiple feeding relationships in an ecosystem.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What is a trophic level?

options.A: The physical location of an organism
options.B: The feeding position an organism occupies in a food chain
options.C: The number of species in an area
options.D: The total biomass of an ecosystem

questions.explanation: A trophic level is the feeding position an organism occupies in a food chain; producers are generally the first trophic level, herbivores the second and successive consumers higher levels.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What is the 10 percent law of energy transfer?

options.A: 100% of energy is transferred to the next trophic level
options.B: Only about 10% of energy at one trophic level is transferred to the next, on average
options.C: 50% of energy is transferred to the next trophic level
options.D: Energy is recycled at each trophic level

questions.explanation: Raymond Lindeman's ecological generalisation states that, on average, only about 10% of energy at one trophic level is transferred to the next; the actual proportion varies.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: Why does energy decrease at successive trophic levels?

options.A: Energy is recycled back to producers
options.B: Organisms use much energy for respiration, movement, growth and maintenance, and much is lost as heat or remains in uneaten/undigested material
options.C: Energy is destroyed completely at each level
options.D: Energy is stored indefinitely in organisms

questions.explanation: Organisms use much of the energy they obtain for respiration, movement, growth and maintenance, and much is lost as heat or remains in uneaten/undigested material.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: In which direction does energy flow in an ecosystem?

options.A: In a cyclic manner and is recycled
options.B: In one direction through trophic levels and is ultimately dissipated as heat

questions.explanation: Energy flows in one direction through trophic levels—from sunlight or chemical energy to producers and consumers—and is ultimately dissipated as heat; it is not recycled.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: Which of the following is true about energy flow in an ecosystem?

options.A: Energy is recycled
options.B: Energy flow is one-way
options.C: Energy increases at each trophic level

questions.explanation: Energy flow is one-way; only about 10% is transferred on average to the next trophic level, and energy is not recycled.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What is an ecological pyramid?

options.A: A graphical representation of the number, biomass or energy of organisms at successive trophic levels
options.B: A network of food chains
options.C: A linear sequence of energy transfer

questions.explanation: An ecological pyramid is a graphical representation of the number, biomass or energy of organisms at successive trophic levels.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What are the three types of ecological pyramids?

options.A: Pyramid of numbers, pyramid of biomass and pyramid of energy
options.B: Pyramid of producers, consumers and decomposers
options.C: Pyramid of herbivores, carnivores and omnivores
options.D: Pyramid of air, water and soil

questions.explanation: The three types are pyramid of numbers, pyramid of biomass and pyramid of energy.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: Which ecological pyramid is always upright?

options.A: Pyramid of numbers
options.B: Pyramid of biomass

questions.explanation: The pyramid of energy is always upright because usable energy decreases at each successive trophic transfer.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: Can a pyramid of numbers be inverted?

options.A: No, it is always upright
options.B: Yes; for example, one tree may support many insects and parasites

questions.explanation: Yes. For example, one tree may support many insects and parasites, producing an inverted or irregular pyramid of numbers.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: Can a pyramid of biomass be inverted?

options.A: No, it is always upright
options.B: Yes; in some aquatic ecosystems, the standing biomass of phytoplankton is lower than that of zooplankton at a given moment

questions.explanation: Yes. In some aquatic ecosystems, the standing biomass of phytoplankton is lower than that of zooplankton at a given moment because phytoplankton reproduce and turn over rapidly.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What is ecological balance?

options.A: A static condition where nothing changes
options.B: A dynamic condition in which interactions and natural processes maintain ecosystem functions and populations within changing limits
options.C: A condition where populations never change
options.D: A condition where only producers exist

questions.explanation: Ecological balance is a dynamic condition in which interactions and natural processes maintain ecosystem functions and populations within changing limits; it does not mean that nature is static.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What is ecological succession?

options.A: A sudden change in species composition
options.B: The gradual change in species composition and community structure in an area over time
options.D: The formation of a food web

questions.explanation: Ecological succession is the gradual change in species composition and community structure in an area over time, often following the formation of new habitat or disturbance.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What is primary succession?

options.A: Succession beginning on a surface without developed soil, such as newly exposed rock or fresh lava
options.B: Succession occurring after a fire where soil remains

questions.explanation: Primary succession begins on a surface without developed soil, such as newly exposed rock or fresh lava.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What is secondary succession?

options.A: Succession beginning on bare rock
options.B: Succession occurring where a community has been disturbed but soil or biological legacies remain
options.D: Succession in a newly formed pond

questions.explanation: Secondary succession occurs where a community has been disturbed but soil or biological legacies remain, such as after a fire or abandoned cultivation.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What is a pioneer species?

options.A: A species that first colonises a newly formed or disturbed habitat and helps modify conditions for later communities
options.B: The last species to arrive in a community
options.C: A species that only lives in climax communities
options.D: A species that never changes its habitat

questions.explanation: A pioneer species first colonises a newly formed or disturbed habitat and helps modify conditions for later communities; lichens and mosses can be pioneers on bare rock.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What is a climax community?

options.A: The first community to colonise bare rock
options.B: A traditional term for a relatively stable late-successional community under a given set of conditions
options.C: A community of only pioneer species

questions.explanation: A climax community is a traditional term for a relatively stable late-successional community under a given set of conditions; modern ecology recognises that communities may remain dynamic and need not reach one fixed climax.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What is a habitat?

options.A: The functional role of a species in an ecosystem
options.B: The natural place or environment in which an organism lives and obtains the conditions and resources it needs
options.C: The feeding position of an organism
options.D: A group of individuals of the same species

questions.explanation: A habitat is the natural place or environment in which an organism lives and obtains the conditions and resources it needs.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What is an ecological niche?

options.A: The physical location where an organism lives
options.B: The functional role of a species in an ecosystem, including resource use, environmental requirements, interactions and position in the food web
options.C: The number of individuals in a population
options.D: The total biomass of an ecosystem

questions.explanation: An ecological niche is the functional role of a species in an ecosystem, including its resource use, environmental requirements, interactions and position in the food web.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What is the difference between habitat and niche?

options.A: Habitat describes how an organism lives; niche describes where it lives
options.B: Habitat describes where an organism lives; niche describes how it lives and functions
options.D: Habitat is for animals; niche is for plants

questions.explanation: Habitat describes where an organism lives; niche describes how it lives and functions, including what it uses and how it interacts.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What is population ecology?

options.A: The study of population size, density, distribution, age structure, growth, birth rates, death rates and migration
options.B: The study of communities only

questions.explanation: Population ecology is the study of population size, density, distribution, age structure, growth, birth rates, death rates and migration.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What is a population?

options.A: All species living in an area
options.B: A group of individuals of the same species living in a particular area at a particular time and potentially interbreeding
options.C: A group of different species interacting
options.D: The non-living components of an area

questions.explanation: A population is a group of individuals of the same species living in a particular area at a particular time and potentially interbreeding.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What is population density?

options.A: The total number of species in an area
options.B: The number of individuals of a population per unit area or volume
options.C: The total biomass of an ecosystem
options.D: The number of trophic levels in a food chain

questions.explanation: Population density is the number of individuals of a population per unit area or volume.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What is a community in ecology?

options.A: A group of individuals of the same species
options.B: All populations of different species living and interacting in a particular area
options.C: The non-living components of an area

questions.explanation: A community in ecology is all populations of different species living and interacting in a particular area.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What is community ecology?

options.A: The study of species composition, diversity, interactions, food webs and changes within ecological communities
options.B: The study of population size only
options.C: The study of individual organisms only
options.D: The study of abiotic factors only

questions.explanation: Community ecology is the study of species composition, diversity, interactions, food webs and changes within ecological communities.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What is mutualism?

options.A: An interaction where one species benefits and the other is harmed
options.B: An interaction where both species benefit (+/+)
options.C: An interaction where one species benefits and the other is unaffected
options.D: An interaction where both species are harmed

questions.explanation: Mutualism is an interaction in which both species benefit; examples include pollinating insects receiving nectar while pollinating flowers.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What is commensalism?

options.A: An interaction where both species benefit
options.B: An interaction where one species benefits and the other is neither significantly helped nor harmed (+/0)
options.C: An interaction where both species are harmed
options.D: An interaction where one species is harmed and the other is unaffected

questions.explanation: Commensalism is an interaction in which one species benefits and the other is neither significantly helped nor harmed; examples often cited include epiphytic orchids growing on trees.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What is parasitism?

options.A: An interaction where both species benefit
options.B: An interaction where one species benefits and the other is unaffected
options.C: An interaction where a parasite benefits while the host is harmed (+/-)
options.D: An interaction where both species are harmed

questions.explanation: Parasitism is an interaction in which a parasite benefits while the host is harmed; examples include tapeworms in humans and ticks on mammals.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What is predation?

options.A: An interaction where both species benefit
options.B: An interaction in which one organism (predator) captures and consumes another (prey)
options.C: An interaction where one species is unaffected
options.D: An interaction where both species are harmed

questions.explanation: Predation is an interaction in which one organism (predator) captures and consumes another (prey).

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What is competition in ecology?

options.A: An interaction where both species benefit
options.B: An interaction in which organisms use the same limited resource, reducing access or success for one or both competitors
options.C: An interaction where one species is unaffected
options.D: An interaction where one species benefits and the other is harmed

questions.explanation: Competition is an interaction in which organisms use the same limited resource, reducing access or success for one or both competitors.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What is symbiosis?

options.A: A close, often long-term association between organisms of different species; it can include mutualism, commensalism or parasitism
options.B: An interaction where both species are harmed

questions.explanation: Symbiosis is a close, often long-term association between organisms of different species; it can include mutualism, commensalism or parasitism depending on the effects.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What is amensalism?

options.A: An interaction where both species benefit
options.B: An interaction in which one species is harmed while the other is not significantly affected; antibiotic release by some microbes is a commonly cited example
options.C: An interaction where one species benefits and the other is harmed
options.D: An interaction where both species are harmed

questions.explanation: Amensalism is an interaction in which one species is harmed while the other is not significantly affected; antibiotic release by some microbes is a commonly cited example.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What is a biome?

options.A: A large ecological region characterised by climate and dominant vegetation or other major biological features
options.B: A small habitat within an ecosystem
options.C: A group of individuals of the same species
options.D: The non-living components of an area

questions.explanation: A biome is a large ecological region characterised by climate and dominant vegetation or other major biological features, such as tropical rainforest, desert, grassland and tundra.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What is the biosphere?

options.A: The global zone of life on Earth, comprising parts of the atmosphere, hydrosphere and lithosphere where organisms occur
options.B: Only the atmosphere

questions.explanation: The biosphere is the global zone of life on Earth, comprising parts of the atmosphere, hydrosphere and lithosphere where organisms occur.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What is a natural resource?

options.A: A material, organism or environmental feature occurring in nature that people or ecosystems use
options.B: Only minerals found underground

questions.explanation: A natural resource is a material, organism or environmental feature occurring in nature that people or ecosystems use, such as water, soil, forests, minerals, sunlight and wind.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What are renewable resources?

options.A: Resources that form much more slowly than they are consumed
options.B: Resources replenished naturally on a human timescale when managed sustainably, such as solar, wind and sustainably harvested biological resources
options.D: Resources that cannot be used by humans

questions.explanation: Renewable resources are replenished naturally on a human timescale when managed sustainably, such as solar, wind and sustainably harvested biological resources.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What are non-renewable resources?

options.A: Resources that are replenished quickly
options.B: Resources that form much more slowly than they are consumed, such as coal, petroleum, natural gas and many mineral deposits
options.D: Resources that are only used for food

questions.explanation: Non-renewable resources form much more slowly than they are consumed, such as coal, petroleum, natural gas and many mineral deposits.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: Are renewable resources inexhaustible?

options.A: Yes, they can never be depleted
options.B: No; they can be depleted or degraded if extraction exceeds their rate of renewal or if ecosystems are damaged

questions.explanation: No. Renewable resources can be depleted or degraded if extraction exceeds their rate of renewal or if ecosystems are damaged.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What are forest resources?

options.A: Only timber and fuelwood
options.B: Goods and ecosystem services supplied by forests, including timber, fuelwood, food, medicines, habitat, carbon storage, soil protection and water regulation

questions.explanation: Forest resources are goods and ecosystem services supplied by forests, including timber, fuelwood, food, medicines, habitat, carbon storage, soil protection and water regulation.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: Why are forests important?

options.A: They only provide timber
options.B: They support biodiversity, store carbon, regulate water cycles, protect soil, reduce erosion and provide livelihoods

questions.explanation: Forests support biodiversity, store carbon, regulate local and regional water cycles, protect soil, reduce erosion and provide livelihoods and resources.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What are water resources?

options.A: Only surface water
options.B: Surface water, groundwater, rainwater, glaciers and other freshwater sources used by people and ecosystems

questions.explanation: Water resources include surface water, groundwater, rainwater, glaciers and other freshwater sources used by people and ecosystems.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What is groundwater?

options.A: Water stored below Earth's surface in saturated soil and rock formations, including aquifers
options.B: Water in rivers and lakes

questions.explanation: Groundwater is water stored below Earth's surface in saturated soil and rock formations, including aquifers.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What is an aquifer?

options.A: A permeable geological formation that can store and transmit usable quantities of groundwater
options.B: A type of soil

questions.explanation: An aquifer is a permeable geological formation that can store and transmit usable quantities of groundwater.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What are soil resources?

options.A: Soil provides a medium for plant growth, stores and filters water, cycles nutrients, supports organisms and underpins agriculture
options.B: Soil is only a source of minerals
options.C: Soil is only a medium for construction

questions.explanation: Soil provides a medium for plant growth, stores and filters water, cycles nutrients, supports organisms and underpins agriculture and terrestrial ecosystems.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What are mineral resources?

options.A: Naturally occurring inorganic substances or deposits that can be extracted for metals, industrial minerals and construction materials
options.B: Only metals

questions.explanation: Mineral resources are naturally occurring inorganic substances or deposits that can be extracted for metals, industrial minerals and construction materials.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What are energy resources?

options.A: Only fossil fuels
options.B: Sources used to produce useful energy, including fossil fuels, nuclear fuels and renewable sources such as solar, wind, hydro, biomass and geothermal energy

questions.explanation: Energy resources are sources used to produce useful energy, including fossil fuels, nuclear fuels and renewable sources such as solar, wind, hydro, biomass and geothermal energy.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What is conservation of natural resources?

options.A: Only protecting forests
options.B: Protection, restoration and careful use of natural resources to maintain their availability, ecological functions and benefits for present and future generations

questions.explanation: Conservation of natural resources is protection, restoration and careful use of natural resources to maintain their availability, ecological functions and benefits for present and future generations.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What is sustainable utilisation?

options.A: Using resources as fast as possible
options.B: Using resources at rates and in ways that maintain ecological integrity and do not undermine the ability of future generations to meet their needs
options.C: Not using any resources at all

questions.explanation: Sustainable utilisation is using resources at rates and in ways that maintain ecological integrity and do not undermine the ability of future generations to meet their needs.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What is deforestation?

options.A: Planting trees in a new area
options.B: Large-scale removal or conversion of forest cover to another land use, such as agriculture, settlement, mining or infrastructure

questions.explanation: Deforestation is large-scale removal or conversion of forest cover to another land use, such as agriculture, settlement, mining or infrastructure.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What are major causes of deforestation?

options.A: Only agricultural expansion
options.B: Agricultural expansion, commercial logging, fuelwood collection, mining, roads, urbanisation, dams, fires and other land-use changes

questions.explanation: Major causes of deforestation include agricultural expansion, commercial logging, fuelwood collection, mining, roads, urbanisation, dams, fires and other land-use changes.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What are major effects of deforestation?

options.A: Only habitat loss
options.B: Habitat loss, biodiversity decline, soil erosion, disrupted water cycles, increased carbon emissions, local climate changes and impacts on forest-dependent communities

questions.explanation: Major effects of deforestation include habitat loss, biodiversity decline, soil erosion, disrupted water cycles, increased carbon emissions, local climate changes and impacts on forest-dependent communities.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What is afforestation?

options.A: Re-establishment of forest on land that was previously forested but has been cleared or degraded
options.B: Establishment of forest on land that has not recently been forested

questions.explanation: Afforestation is the establishment of forest on land that has not recently been forested, according to the definition used by the relevant programme or inventory.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What is reforestation?

options.A: Establishment of forest on land that has not recently been forested
options.B: Re-establishment of forest on land that was previously forested but has been cleared or degraded

questions.explanation: Reforestation is the re-establishment of forest on land that was previously forested but has been cleared or degraded.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What is the difference between afforestation and reforestation?

options.A: Afforestation creates forest on land not recently forested; reforestation restores forest on previously forested land
options.B: Afforestation restores forest on previously forested land; reforestation creates forest on land not recently forested
options.D: Afforestation is for timber; reforestation is for wildlife

questions.explanation: Afforestation creates forest on land not recently forested; reforestation restores forest on previously forested land.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What is soil erosion?

options.A: The formation of new soil
options.B: The detachment and movement of topsoil by water, wind, ice or human activity

questions.explanation: Soil erosion is the detachment and movement of topsoil by water, wind, ice or human activity.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What are major causes of soil erosion?

options.A: Only deforestation
options.B: Removal of vegetation, overgrazing, deforestation, inappropriate cultivation, construction, mining, intense rainfall and wind

questions.explanation: Major causes of soil erosion include removal of vegetation, overgrazing, deforestation, inappropriate cultivation, construction, mining, intense rainfall and wind.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: How can soil erosion be controlled?

options.A: By removing all vegetation
options.B: Maintain vegetation cover, practise contour ploughing and terracing, use cover crops and mulching, build check dams, manage grazing and protect riparian zones

questions.explanation: Soil erosion can be controlled by maintaining vegetation cover, practising contour ploughing and terracing, using cover crops and mulching, building check dams, managing grazing and protecting riparian zones.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What is watershed management?

options.A: Integrated management of land, water and vegetation within a drainage area to conserve soil and water, reduce runoff and improve livelihoods and ecosystem health
options.B: Management of a single river only

questions.explanation: Watershed management is integrated management of land, water and vegetation within a drainage area to conserve soil and water, reduce runoff and improve livelihoods and ecosystem health.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What is a watershed?

options.A: An area of land from which all surface runoff drains to a common outlet, such as a stream, lake or river
options.B: A type of aquifer

questions.explanation: A watershed is an area of land from which all surface runoff drains to a common outlet, such as a stream, lake or river.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What is rainwater harvesting?

options.A: Collection and storage of rainwater from rooftops or land surfaces for later use or to recharge groundwater
options.B: Collection of river water

questions.explanation: Rainwater harvesting is the collection and storage of rainwater from rooftops or land surfaces for later use or to recharge groundwater.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What are common rainwater-harvesting methods?

options.A: Only rooftop collection
options.B: Rooftop collection into tanks, recharge pits, recharge wells, percolation tanks, check dams, farm ponds and contour bunds

questions.explanation: Common rainwater-harvesting methods include rooftop collection into tanks, recharge pits, recharge wells, percolation tanks, check dams, farm ponds and contour bunds.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: Why is groundwater conservation important?

options.A: It helps maintain drinking-water supplies, irrigation, river baselines and ecosystem functions and reduces the risk of falling water tables and land subsidence
options.B: It only helps in agriculture

questions.explanation: Groundwater conservation helps maintain drinking-water supplies, irrigation, river baselines and ecosystem functions and reduces the risk of falling water tables and land subsidence.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: How can groundwater be conserved?

options.A: By increasing extraction
options.B: Recharge aquifers, protect wetlands and recharge zones, reduce leakage, use water-efficient irrigation, regulate extraction and reuse treated wastewater where safe

questions.explanation: Groundwater can be conserved by recharging aquifers, protecting wetlands and recharge zones, reducing leakage, using water-efficient irrigation, regulating extraction and reusing treated wastewater where safe.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What is sustainable forest management?

options.A: Management that maintains forest biodiversity, productivity, regeneration, ecological processes and social benefits over time
options.B: Management that maximises timber extraction
options.C: Management that eliminates all human use
options.D: Management that converts forests to agriculture

questions.explanation: Sustainable forest management maintains forest biodiversity, productivity, regeneration, ecological processes and social benefits over time.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What is the 3R principle in resource conservation?

options.A: Reduce, Reuse and Recycle; reduction is generally preferred before recycling
options.B: Remove, Replace and Restore

questions.explanation: The 3R principle is Reduce consumption and waste, Reuse products and materials, and Recycle materials into useful products; reduction is generally preferred before recycling.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What is biodiversity?

options.A: The variety and variability of life, including diversity within species, between species and among ecosystems
options.B: Only the number of species in an area

questions.explanation: Biodiversity is the variety and variability of life, including diversity within species, between species and among ecosystems.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What are the three main levels of biodiversity?

options.A: Genetic diversity, species diversity and ecosystem diversity
options.B: Plant diversity, animal diversity and microbial diversity

questions.explanation: The three main levels of biodiversity are genetic diversity, species diversity and ecosystem diversity.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What is species diversity?

options.A: The variety of species in an area and their relative abundance; it includes species richness and evenness
options.B: Only the number of species in an area

questions.explanation: Species diversity is the variety of species in an area and their relative abundance; it includes species richness and evenness.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What is ecosystem diversity?

options.A: The variety of genes within a species
options.B: The variety of habitats, ecological communities and ecosystem processes across a region
options.C: The number of species in an area

questions.explanation: Ecosystem diversity is the variety of habitats, ecological communities and ecosystem processes across a region.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: Why is biodiversity important?

options.A: It only provides food
options.B: It supports ecosystem functioning and resilience and provides food, medicines, pollination, soil formation, water purification, climate regulation, cultural values and livelihoods

questions.explanation: Biodiversity supports ecosystem functioning and resilience and provides food, medicines, pollination, soil formation, water purification, climate regulation, cultural values and livelihoods.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What is a biodiversity hotspot?

options.A: A biogeographic region with exceptional plant endemism and severe habitat loss
options.B: Any area with many species
options.D: A region with no endemic species

questions.explanation: A biodiversity hotspot is a biogeographic region with exceptional plant endemism and severe habitat loss; the Conservation International criteria require at least 1,500 endemic vascular plant species and loss of at least 70% of original natural vegetation.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What are the criteria for a biodiversity hotspot under Conservation International?

options.A: At least 1,500 endemic vascular plant species and at least 70% loss of original natural vegetation
options.B: At least 500 endemic species and 50% habitat loss
options.C: At least 2,000 endemic species and 80% habitat loss
options.D: At least 100 endemic species and 30% habitat loss

questions.explanation: The Conservation International criteria require at least 1,500 endemic vascular plant species and loss of at least 70% of original natural vegetation.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: How many global biodiversity hotspots are commonly recognised in the current Conservation International framework?
questions.explanation: 36 biodiversity hotspots are commonly recognised in the current Conservation International framework.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: Which biodiversity hotspots include parts of India?

options.A: Himalaya, Indo-Burma, Western Ghats-Sri Lanka and Sundaland
options.B: Only Himalaya

questions.explanation: India lies within four biodiversity hotspots: the Himalaya, Indo-Burma, Western Ghats-Sri Lanka and Sundaland; the Nicobar Islands are part of Sundaland.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: The Nicobar Islands are part of which biodiversity hotspot?

options.A: Himalaya
options.B: Indo-Burma

questions.explanation: The Nicobar Islands are part of the Sundaland hotspot.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What is an endemic species?

options.A: A species found everywhere in the world
options.B: A species naturally restricted to a particular geographic area and found nowhere else in the wild

questions.explanation: An endemic species is naturally restricted to a particular geographic area and found nowhere else in the wild.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What is an endangered species?

options.A: A species facing a very high risk of extinction in the wild, corresponding to IUCN Red List category Endangered (EN)
options.B: A species with no risk of extinction

questions.explanation: An endangered species faces a very high risk of extinction in the wild, corresponding to the IUCN Red List category Endangered (EN).

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What is a vulnerable species?

options.A: A species facing a very high risk of extinction
options.B: A species facing a high risk of extinction in the wild, corresponding to IUCN category Vulnerable (VU)
options.C: A species with no risk of extinction
options.D: A species that is already extinct

questions.explanation: A vulnerable species faces a high risk of extinction in the wild, corresponding to the IUCN category Vulnerable (VU).

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What is an extinct species?

options.A: A species facing a high risk of extinction
options.B: A species for which there is no reasonable doubt that the last individual has died, corresponding to IUCN category Extinct (EX)
options.C: A species found in zoos only

questions.explanation: An extinct species is one for which there is no reasonable doubt that the last individual has died, corresponding to IUCN category Extinct (EX).

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What are threatened species under the IUCN system?

options.A: Species classified as Least Concern or Near Threatened
options.B: Species classified as Vulnerable (VU), Endangered (EN) or Critically Endangered (CR)
options.C: Species classified as Data Deficient only

questions.explanation: Threatened species under the IUCN system are classified as Vulnerable (VU), Endangered (EN) or Critically Endangered (CR).

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What is the IUCN Red List?

options.A: A list of protected areas in India
options.B: The International Union for Conservation of Nature's global assessment system that evaluates extinction risk of species using defined criteria
options.C: A list of invasive species only
options.D: A list of medicinal plants only

questions.explanation: The IUCN Red List is the International Union for Conservation of Nature's global assessment system that evaluates extinction risk of species using defined criteria.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What are the main IUCN Red List categories?

options.A: Not Evaluated (NE), Data Deficient (DD), Least Concern (LC), Near Threatened (NT), Vulnerable (VU), Endangered (EN), Critically Endangered (CR), Extinct in the Wild (EW) and Extinct (EX)
options.B: Only Vulnerable, Endangered and Critically Endangered
options.C: Only Least Concern and Near Threatened
options.D: Only Extinct and Extinct in the Wild

questions.explanation: The main IUCN Red List categories are Not Evaluated (NE), Data Deficient (DD), Least Concern (LC), Near Threatened (NT), Vulnerable (VU), Endangered (EN), Critically Endangered (CR), Extinct in the Wild (EW) and Extinct (EX).

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: Does Data Deficient mean a species is safe?

options.A: Yes, it means low risk
options.B: No; Data Deficient means available information is insufficient to assess extinction risk; it does not mean low risk
options.C: Yes, it means the species is extinct
options.D: Yes, it means the species is invasive

questions.explanation: No. Data Deficient means available information is insufficient to assess extinction risk; it does not mean low risk.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What is wildlife conservation?

options.A: Protection and management of wild species and their habitats to maintain viable populations, ecological roles and genetic diversity
options.B: Only protecting tigers

questions.explanation: Wildlife conservation is the protection and management of wild species and their habitats to maintain viable populations, ecological roles and genetic diversity.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What is in-situ conservation?

options.A: Conservation of species outside natural habitats
options.B: Conservation of species in their natural habitats, for example through national parks, wildlife sanctuaries, biosphere reserves and community reserves

questions.explanation: In-situ conservation is the conservation of species in their natural habitats, for example through national parks, wildlife sanctuaries, biosphere reserves and community reserves.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What is ex-situ conservation?

options.A: Conservation of species in their natural habitats
options.B: Conservation outside natural habitats, such as in zoos, botanical gardens, seed banks, gene banks, tissue culture collections and captive-breeding programmes

questions.explanation: Ex-situ conservation is conservation outside natural habitats, such as in zoos, botanical gardens, seed banks, gene banks, tissue culture collections and captive-breeding programmes.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What is a national park in India?

options.A: A protected area notified under the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972, with stronger restrictions on activities than many other protected-area categories
options.B: A protected area under the Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980
options.C: A protected area under the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986
options.D: A protected area under the Biological Diversity Act, 2002

questions.explanation: A national park in India is a protected area notified under the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972, with stronger restrictions on activities than many other protected-area categories; exact legal provisions and permitted rights are governed by the Act.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What is a wildlife sanctuary in India?

options.A: A protected area declared under the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972, for protecting wildlife and habitat
options.B: A protected area under the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986
options.C: A protected area under the Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980
options.D: A protected area under the Biological Diversity Act, 2002

questions.explanation: A wildlife sanctuary in India is a protected area declared under the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972, for protecting wildlife and habitat, subject to the Act's restrictions and applicable rights/permissions.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What is a biosphere reserve?

options.A: A large landscape designated under UNESCO's Man and the Biosphere Programme to promote biodiversity conservation alongside sustainable development and research
options.B: A protected area under the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972
options.C: A protected area under the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986
options.D: A protected area under the Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980

questions.explanation: A biosphere reserve is a large landscape designated under UNESCO's Man and the Biosphere Programme to promote biodiversity conservation alongside sustainable development and research; it commonly has core, buffer and transition zones.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What are the three zones of a biosphere reserve?

options.A: Core zone, buffer zone and transition zone
options.B: Inner zone, middle zone and outer zone
options.C: Protected zone, use zone and restoration zone
options.D: Forest zone, water zone and soil zone

questions.explanation: The three zones of a biosphere reserve are core zone for strict conservation, buffer zone for compatible activities such as research and education, and transition zone where sustainable human activities occur.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What is the purpose of the core zone of a biosphere reserve?

options.A: For strict conservation
options.B: For sustainable human activities

questions.explanation: The core zone of a biosphere reserve is for strict conservation.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What is the purpose of the transition zone of a biosphere reserve?

options.A: For strict conservation
options.B: For sustainable human activities

questions.explanation: The transition zone of a biosphere reserve is where sustainable human activities occur.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What is a botanical garden?

options.A: A managed collection of living plants maintained for research, education, conservation and public display
options.B: A facility that keeps wild animals

questions.explanation: A botanical garden is a managed collection of living plants maintained for research, education, conservation and public display.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What is a zoological park?

options.A: A managed collection of living plants
options.B: A facility that keeps wild animals in managed conditions for conservation, education, research and, in some cases, breeding

questions.explanation: A zoological park is a facility that keeps wild animals in managed conditions for conservation, education, research and, in some cases, breeding.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What is a wildlife corridor?

options.A: A strip or network of habitat connecting separated habitat patches and allowing movement of organisms, gene flow and access to resources
options.B: A protected area under the Wildlife (Protection) Act

questions.explanation: A wildlife corridor is a strip or network of habitat connecting separated habitat patches and allowing movement of organisms, gene flow and access to resources.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What is human-wildlife conflict?

options.A: Negative interactions between people and wild animals, such as crop damage, livestock predation, property damage, injury or loss of human life
options.B: A type of conservation strategy

questions.explanation: Human-wildlife conflict refers to negative interactions between people and wild animals, such as crop damage, livestock predation, property damage, injury or loss of human life.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: How can human-wildlife conflict be reduced?

options.A: Protect and restore habitats and corridors, use locally appropriate barriers and early-warning systems, secure crops and livestock, manage waste and provide fair, timely compensation and community participation
options.B: By eliminating all wildlife

questions.explanation: Human-wildlife conflict can be reduced by protecting and restoring habitats and corridors, using locally appropriate barriers and early-warning systems, securing crops and livestock, managing waste and providing fair, timely compensation and community participation.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What is an invasive alien species?

options.A: A native species that is common

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What is the difference between an alien species and an invasive species?

options.A: An alien species occurs outside its natural range due to human activity or other introduction; it is termed invasive when it spreads and causes or is likely to cause harm

options.C: An alien species is always harmful

questions.explanation: An alien species occurs outside its natural range due to human activity or other introduction; it is termed invasive when it spreads and causes or is likely to cause harm.

questions.question: What is the scientific name of water hyacinth (formerly Eichhornia crassipes)?

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What is the importance of biodiversity conservation in India?

options.A: India contains diverse ecosystems and high species richness and endemism; conservation supports ecological services, livelihoods, cultural values and resilience to environmental change

options.D: Biodiversity has no role in India

questions.question: What are examples of India's major biodiversity-rich regions?

options.B: Only the Western Ghats
options.D: Only the Andaman and Nicobar Islands

questions.explanation: Examples of India's major biodiversity-rich regions include the Himalaya, Western Ghats, north-eastern India, Andaman and Nicobar Islands, forests of central India, deserts, wetlands, coasts and marine ecosystems.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: Why are the Western Ghats important for biodiversity?

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What is the lion-tailed macaque?

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What is the importance of protected areas in Karnataka?

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What is a seed bank?

options.B: A facility that stores animal genetic material only

questions.explanation: A seed bank is a facility that stores seeds under controlled conditions to conserve plant genetic resources for future use, research and restoration.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What is captive breeding?

options.A: Managed breeding of threatened animals outside or within protected settings to support conservation, genetic management and possible reintroduction
options.B: Breeding of crops only
