questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What is environmental pollution?

options.A: Undesirable change in the physical, chemical or biological characteristics of air, water or land that harms organisms, ecosystems or human health
options.B: Only air pollution

questions.explanation: Environmental pollution is an undesirable change in the physical, chemical or biological characteristics of air, water or land that harms organisms, ecosystems or human health.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What is air pollution?

options.A: Contamination of the atmosphere by harmful gases, particles or biological materials at concentrations that can affect health or the environment
options.B: Only contamination by gases

questions.explanation: Air pollution is contamination of the atmosphere by harmful gases, particles or biological materials at concentrations that can affect health or the environment.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What are major air pollutants?

options.A: Particulate matter (PM2.5 and PM10), sulphur dioxide, nitrogen oxides, carbon monoxide, ground-level ozone, volatile organic compounds, ammonia, lead and certain toxic air pollutants
options.B: Only particulate matter

questions.explanation: Major air pollutants include particulate matter (PM2.5 and PM10), sulphur dioxide, nitrogen oxides, carbon monoxide, ground-level ozone, volatile organic compounds, ammonia, lead and certain toxic air pollutants.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What are PM2.5 and PM10?

options.A: Particulate matter with aerodynamic diameters of 2.5 micrometres or less and 10 micrometres or less, respectively; fine particles can penetrate deep into the lungs
options.B: Gases with molecular weights of 2.5 and 10

questions.explanation: PM2.5 and PM10 are particulate matter with aerodynamic diameters of 2.5 micrometres or less and 10 micrometres or less, respectively; fine particles can penetrate deep into the lungs.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What are major sources of air pollution?

options.A: Vehicle exhaust, power plants, industries, construction and road dust, waste burning, household solid fuels, agricultural residue burning and natural sources such as dust storms and wildfires
options.B: Only vehicle exhaust

questions.explanation: Major sources of air pollution include vehicle exhaust, power plants, industries, construction and road dust, waste burning, household solid fuels, agricultural residue burning and natural sources such as dust storms and wildfires.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What are effects of air pollution?

options.A: Respiratory and cardiovascular disease, premature mortality, reduced visibility, crop damage, ecosystem acidification and climate effects depending on the pollutant
options.B: Only respiratory disease

questions.explanation: Effects of air pollution include respiratory and cardiovascular disease, premature mortality, reduced visibility, crop damage, ecosystem acidification and climate effects depending on the pollutant.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What is water pollution?

options.A: Contamination or alteration of water quality that makes it harmful or unsuitable for drinking, aquatic life, agriculture or other uses
options.B: Only contamination by sewage

questions.explanation: Water pollution is contamination or alteration of water quality that makes it harmful or unsuitable for drinking, aquatic life, agriculture or other uses.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What are common water pollutants?

options.A: Pathogens, sewage, nutrients such as nitrates and phosphates, pesticides, industrial chemicals, heavy metals, oil, plastics, sediments and heat
options.B: Only pathogens

questions.explanation: Common water pollutants include pathogens, sewage, nutrients such as nitrates and phosphates, pesticides, industrial chemicals, heavy metals, oil, plastics, sediments and heat.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What is eutrophication?

options.A: Excess nutrient enrichment of water, often by nitrogen and phosphorus, causing excessive algal or plant growth and sometimes oxygen depletion and fish kills
options.B: Depletion of nutrients in water
options.C: Increase in oxygen levels in water

questions.explanation: Eutrophication is excess nutrient enrichment of water, often by nitrogen and phosphorus, causing excessive algal or plant growth and sometimes oxygen depletion and fish kills.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What is biochemical oxygen demand (BOD)?

options.A: The amount of dissolved oxygen used by microorganisms to break down biodegradable organic matter in a water sample under specified test conditions; high BOD often indicates organic pollution
options.B: The amount of oxygen produced by photosynthesis
options.C: The amount of oxygen required for chemical oxidation only
options.D: The amount of oxygen in the atmosphere

questions.explanation: BOD is the amount of dissolved oxygen used by microorganisms to break down biodegradable organic matter in a water sample under specified test conditions; high BOD often indicates organic pollution.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What is chemical oxygen demand (COD)?

options.A: An analytical measure of the oxygen equivalent required to chemically oxidise substances in water; it is often used as an indicator of pollution load
options.B: The amount of oxygen used by microorganisms
options.C: The amount of oxygen produced by plants
options.D: The amount of oxygen in the atmosphere

questions.explanation: COD is an analytical measure of the oxygen equivalent required to chemically oxidise substances in water; it is often used as an indicator of pollution load.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What is soil pollution?

options.A: Contamination of soil by harmful chemicals, salts, pathogens or wastes at levels that damage soil function, organisms, crops or human health
options.B: Only contamination by pesticides

questions.explanation: Soil pollution is contamination of soil by harmful chemicals, salts, pathogens or wastes at levels that damage soil function, organisms, crops or human health.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What are common causes of soil pollution?

options.A: Excessive pesticides and fertilisers, industrial waste, mining, oil spills, landfill leakage, sewage sludge contamination and improper disposal of hazardous waste
options.B: Only excessive pesticides

questions.explanation: Common causes of soil pollution include excessive pesticides and fertilisers, industrial waste, mining, oil spills, landfill leakage, sewage sludge contamination and improper disposal of hazardous waste.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What is noise pollution?

options.A: Unwanted or excessive sound that can harm health or interfere with normal activities and wildlife
options.B: Only loud music

questions.explanation: Noise pollution is unwanted or excessive sound that can harm health or interfere with normal activities and wildlife.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What are effects of prolonged noise exposure?

options.A: Hearing loss, sleep disturbance, stress, impaired concentration and cardiovascular effects; wildlife communication and behaviour can also be disrupted
options.B: Only hearing loss

questions.explanation: Effects of prolonged noise exposure include hearing loss, sleep disturbance, stress, impaired concentration and cardiovascular effects; wildlife communication and behaviour can also be disrupted.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What is thermal pollution?

options.A: Undesirable change in the temperature of a natural water body, often from discharge of heated industrial or power-station cooling water, which can reduce dissolved oxygen and stress aquatic organisms
options.B: Pollution caused by cold water

questions.explanation: Thermal pollution is an undesirable change in the temperature of a natural water body, often from discharge of heated industrial or power-station cooling water, which can reduce dissolved oxygen and stress aquatic organisms.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What is radioactive pollution?

options.A: Presence or release of radioactive substances or ionising radiation in the environment at levels that can cause harmful exposure
options.B: Pollution caused by sound

questions.explanation: Radioactive pollution is the presence or release of radioactive substances or ionising radiation in the environment at levels that can cause harmful exposure.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What is marine pollution?

options.A: Introduction of harmful substances or energy into seas and oceans, including plastics, oil, sewage, nutrients, chemicals, noise and heat
options.B: Only plastic pollution

questions.explanation: Marine pollution is the introduction of harmful substances or energy into seas and oceans, including plastics, oil, sewage, nutrients, chemicals, noise and heat.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What is plastic pollution?

options.A: Accumulation of plastic materials in the environment, where they can injure wildlife, fragment into smaller particles and persist for long periods
options.B: Only plastic in oceans

questions.explanation: Plastic pollution is the accumulation of plastic materials in the environment, where they can injure wildlife, fragment into smaller particles and persist for long periods.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What are microplastics?

options.A: Plastic particles generally smaller than 5 millimetres; they may be manufactured at small sizes or form when larger plastics fragment
options.B: Plastic particles larger than 10 centimetres
options.C: Only plastic particles found in the atmosphere
options.D: Only plastic particles found in soil

questions.explanation: Microplastics are plastic particles generally smaller than 5 millimetres; they may be manufactured at small sizes or form when larger plastics fragment.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What is industrial pollution?

options.A: Pollution arising from industrial processes, including emissions, wastewater, solid residues, hazardous chemicals, heat and noise
options.B: Only air emissions from industries

questions.explanation: Industrial pollution arises from industrial processes, including emissions, wastewater, solid residues, hazardous chemicals, heat and noise.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What is agricultural pollution?

options.A: Environmental contamination from farming, including nutrient runoff, pesticides, soil erosion, livestock waste, salinity and agricultural plastic waste
options.B: Only pesticide pollution

questions.explanation: Agricultural pollution is environmental contamination from farming, including nutrient runoff, pesticides, soil erosion, livestock waste, salinity and agricultural plastic waste.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What is domestic waste pollution?

options.A: Pollution from household sewage, detergents, food waste, plastics, oils, medicines and other discarded materials
options.B: Only sewage pollution

questions.explanation: Domestic waste pollution is pollution from household sewage, detergents, food waste, plastics, oils, medicines and other discarded materials.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What is pollution prevention?

options.A: Avoiding or reducing pollutants at their source through cleaner production, efficient resource use, safer substitutes, process control and good waste management
options.B: Treating pollution after it is generated

questions.explanation: Pollution prevention is avoiding or reducing pollutants at their source through cleaner production, efficient resource use, safer substitutes, process control and good waste management.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What is wastewater treatment?

options.A: Physical, biological and chemical processes used to remove solids, organic matter, nutrients, pathogens and other contaminants from wastewater
options.B: Only physical processes

questions.explanation: Wastewater treatment involves physical, biological and chemical processes used to remove solids, organic matter, nutrients, pathogens and other contaminants from wastewater.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What are the usual stages of sewage treatment?

options.A: Preliminary treatment (screens and grit removal), primary settling, secondary biological treatment and, where needed, tertiary/advanced treatment and disinfection
options.B: Only primary and secondary treatment

questions.explanation: The usual stages of sewage treatment are preliminary treatment (screens and grit removal), primary settling, secondary biological treatment and, where needed, tertiary/advanced treatment and disinfection.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What happens during primary sewage treatment?

options.A: Physical processes such as screening and sedimentation remove large solids, grit and settleable suspended matter
options.B: Microorganisms break down organic matter

questions.explanation: During primary sewage treatment, physical processes such as screening and sedimentation remove large solids, grit and settleable suspended matter.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What happens during secondary sewage treatment?

options.A: Microorganisms biologically break down dissolved and suspended biodegradable organic matter, commonly in activated-sludge or biofilm systems
options.B: Large solids are removed by screening
options.C: Nutrients are removed by chemical precipitation

questions.explanation: During secondary sewage treatment, microorganisms biologically break down dissolved and suspended biodegradable organic matter, commonly in activated-sludge or biofilm systems.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What is tertiary sewage treatment?

options.A: Additional treatment to remove nutrients, remaining suspended solids, dissolved contaminants or pathogens, depending on the intended discharge or reuse
options.B: Primary settling

questions.explanation: Tertiary sewage treatment is additional treatment to remove nutrients, remaining suspended solids, dissolved contaminants or pathogens, depending on the intended discharge or reuse.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What is solid waste management?

options.A: Systematic segregation, collection, storage, transport, processing, recovery and safe disposal of solid waste
options.B: Only collection and disposal

questions.explanation: Solid waste management is the systematic segregation, collection, storage, transport, processing, recovery and safe disposal of solid waste.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What is biomedical waste?

options.A: Waste generated during diagnosis, treatment or immunisation of humans or animals, or in related research and biological production/testing, requiring regulated segregation and treatment
options.B: Only waste from hospitals

questions.explanation: Biomedical waste is waste generated during diagnosis, treatment or immunisation of humans or animals, or in related research and biological production/testing, requiring regulated segregation and treatment.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What is e-waste?

options.A: Discarded electrical and electronic equipment and its components; it may contain valuable materials as well as hazardous substances
options.B: Only discarded computers

questions.explanation: E-waste is discarded electrical and electronic equipment and its components; it may contain valuable materials as well as hazardous substances.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What is hazardous waste?

options.A: Waste with properties such as toxicity, corrosivity, ignitability or reactivity that can pose substantial risks to health or the environment and requires special handling
options.B: Only toxic waste

questions.explanation: Hazardous waste has properties such as toxicity, corrosivity, ignitability or reactivity that can pose substantial risks to health or the environment and requires special handling.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What is plastic waste management?

options.A: Prevention, segregation, collection, reuse, recycling, processing and environmentally sound disposal of discarded plastic, supported by producer responsibility and design improvements
options.B: Only recycling

questions.explanation: Plastic waste management includes prevention, segregation, collection, reuse, recycling, processing and environmentally sound disposal of discarded plastic, supported by producer responsibility and design improvements.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What does the 3R principle mean in waste management?

options.A: Reduce, Reuse and Recycle; reducing consumption and waste is generally the first priority
options.B: Remove, Replace and Restore

questions.explanation: The 3R principle means Reduce, Reuse and Recycle; reducing consumption and waste is generally the first priority.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What is composting?

options.A: Controlled biological decomposition of organic waste into a stable, soil-like material that can improve soil structure and nutrient content
options.B: Burning of organic waste

questions.explanation: Composting is the controlled biological decomposition of organic waste into a stable, soil-like material that can improve soil structure and nutrient content.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What is biodegradable waste?

options.A: Waste that microorganisms can break down into simpler substances under suitable conditions, such as food scraps, leaves and many paper products
options.B: Waste that cannot be broken down by microorganisms

questions.explanation: Biodegradable waste is waste that microorganisms can break down into simpler substances under suitable conditions, such as food scraps, leaves and many paper products.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: Is biodegradable waste always harmless?

options.A: Yes, it is always harmless
options.B: No; poorly managed biodegradable waste can generate methane, leachate, odours and pathogens; management conditions matter

questions.explanation: No. Poorly managed biodegradable waste can generate methane, leachate, odours and pathogens; management conditions matter.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What is the waste hierarchy?

options.A: A preferred order of waste management: prevention/reduction, preparing for reuse, recycling, recovery and, as a last resort, disposal
options.B: A list of waste types

questions.explanation: The waste hierarchy is a preferred order of waste management: prevention/reduction, preparing for reuse, recycling, recovery and, as a last resort, disposal.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What is leachate?

options.A: Liquid that has percolated through waste and carries dissolved or suspended contaminants; it must be collected and treated at engineered landfills
options.B: A type of gas from landfills

questions.explanation: Leachate is liquid that has percolated through waste and carries dissolved or suspended contaminants; it must be collected and treated at engineered landfills.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What is a sanitary landfill?

options.A: An engineered facility where waste is placed, compacted and covered with systems for leachate and gas management and environmental monitoring
options.B: An open dumping ground

questions.explanation: A sanitary landfill is an engineered facility where waste is placed, compacted and covered with systems for leachate and gas management and environmental monitoring.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What is the atmosphere?

options.A: The layer of gases surrounding Earth, held by gravity and essential for climate, weather and life
options.B: Only the ozone layer

questions.explanation: The atmosphere is the layer of gases surrounding Earth, held by gravity and essential for climate, weather and life.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What is the approximate composition of dry air near Earth's surface?

options.A: About 78.08% nitrogen, 20.95% oxygen, 0.93% argon and about 0.04% carbon dioxide, with trace gases
options.B: About 50% nitrogen and 50% oxygen

questions.explanation: Dry air near Earth's surface is about 78.08% nitrogen, 20.95% oxygen, 0.93% argon and about 0.04% carbon dioxide, with trace gases; water vapour varies.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What are the main layers of the atmosphere?

options.A: Troposphere, stratosphere, mesosphere, thermosphere and exosphere
options.B: Troposphere, stratosphere and mesosphere only

questions.explanation: The main layers of the atmosphere are troposphere, stratosphere, mesosphere, thermosphere and exosphere, based mainly on temperature structure.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: In which atmospheric layer does most weather occur?

options.A: Troposphere
options.B: Stratosphere

questions.explanation: Most weather occurs in the troposphere, the lowest atmospheric layer.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: In which layer is the ozone layer concentrated?

options.A: Troposphere
options.B: Stratosphere, mainly around 15-35 km altitude

questions.explanation: The ozone layer is concentrated in the stratosphere, mainly around 15-35 km altitude, though ozone is distributed over a wider range.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What is weather?

options.A: The long-term statistical pattern of weather in a region
options.B: The short-term state of the atmosphere at a particular place and time, including temperature, rainfall, wind, humidity and cloud cover

questions.explanation: Weather is the short-term state of the atmosphere at a particular place and time, including temperature, rainfall, wind, humidity and cloud cover.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What is climate?

options.A: The short-term state of the atmosphere
options.B: The long-term statistical pattern of weather in a region, commonly assessed over periods of about 30 years or more

questions.explanation: Climate is the long-term statistical pattern of weather in a region, commonly assessed over periods of about 30 years or more.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What is the greenhouse effect?

options.A: Cooling of Earth's surface due to greenhouse gases
options.B: Warming of Earth's surface and lower atmosphere because greenhouse gases absorb and re-emit infrared radiation emitted by Earth

questions.explanation: The greenhouse effect is the warming of Earth's surface and lower atmosphere because greenhouse gases absorb and re-emit infrared radiation emitted by Earth.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: Name the major greenhouse gases.

options.A: Water vapour, carbon dioxide, methane, nitrous oxide, ozone and fluorinated gases such as hydrofluorocarbons, perfluorocarbons, sulphur hexafluoride and nitrogen trifluoride
options.B: Only carbon dioxide

questions.explanation: Major greenhouse gases include water vapour, carbon dioxide, methane, nitrous oxide, ozone and fluorinated gases such as hydrofluorocarbons, perfluorocarbons, sulphur hexafluoride and nitrogen trifluoride.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: Is the natural greenhouse effect necessary for life?

options.A: No, it is harmful
options.B: Yes; the natural greenhouse effect keeps Earth much warmer than it would otherwise be; human emissions are strengthening it and causing additional warming
options.C: No, it has no effect on temperature

questions.explanation: Yes. The natural greenhouse effect keeps Earth much warmer than it would otherwise be; human emissions are strengthening it and causing additional warming.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What is global warming?

options.A: The long-term increase in Earth's average surface temperature, primarily driven in the modern era by human-caused greenhouse-gas emissions
options.B: A short-term increase in temperature
options.D: The depletion of the ozone layer

questions.explanation: Global warming is the long-term increase in Earth's average surface temperature, primarily driven in the modern era by human-caused greenhouse-gas emissions.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What is climate change?

options.A: Only changes in temperature
options.B: Long-term changes in climate patterns, including temperature, precipitation, sea level and extremes, caused by natural factors and human activities; recent global warming is predominantly human-caused

questions.explanation: Climate change refers to long-term changes in climate patterns, including temperature, precipitation, sea level and extremes, caused by natural factors and human activities; recent global warming is predominantly human-caused.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What is a carbon footprint?

options.A: The total greenhouse-gas emissions associated with an individual, product, organisation, activity or event, usually expressed as carbon dioxide equivalent (CO2e)
options.B: The physical footprint of a carbon atom
options.C: The amount of carbon in soil
options.D: The amount of carbon in the atmosphere

questions.explanation: A carbon footprint is the total greenhouse-gas emissions associated with an individual, product, organisation, activity or event, usually expressed as carbon dioxide equivalent (CO2e).

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What is the carbon cycle?

options.A: The movement of carbon among the atmosphere, oceans, living organisms, soils, rocks and fossil fuels through processes such as photosynthesis, respiration, decomposition, ocean exchange and combustion
options.B: The movement of carbon only in the atmosphere
options.C: The movement of carbon only in the oceans
options.D: The movement of carbon only in living organisms

questions.explanation: The carbon cycle is the movement of carbon among the atmosphere, oceans, living organisms, soils, rocks and fossil fuels through processes such as photosynthesis, respiration, decomposition, ocean exchange and combustion.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What is carbon sequestration?

options.A: Capture and long-term storage of carbon dioxide or carbon in vegetation, soils, oceans, geological formations or engineered systems
options.B: Release of carbon dioxide into the atmosphere

questions.explanation: Carbon sequestration is the capture and long-term storage of carbon dioxide or carbon in vegetation, soils, oceans, geological formations or engineered systems.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What is the ozone layer?

options.A: A region of the troposphere with high ozone concentration
options.B: A region of the stratosphere with relatively high ozone concentration that absorbs most harmful solar ultraviolet-B and ultraviolet-C radiation

questions.explanation: The ozone layer is a region of the stratosphere with relatively high ozone concentration that absorbs most harmful solar ultraviolet-B and ultraviolet-C radiation.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What causes ozone-layer depletion?

options.A: Carbon dioxide emissions
options.B: Ozone-depleting substances such as CFCs and halons release chlorine or bromine in the stratosphere, catalytically destroying ozone

questions.explanation: Ozone-depleting substances such as CFCs and halons release chlorine or bromine in the stratosphere, catalytically destroying ozone.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What are the effects of ozone depletion?

options.A: More harmful UV-B can reach Earth's surface, increasing risks of skin cancer, cataracts and immune effects and harming crops, phytoplankton and ecosystems
options.B: Only skin cancer

questions.explanation: Effects of ozone depletion include more harmful UV-B reaching Earth's surface, increasing risks of skin cancer, cataracts and immune effects and harming crops, phytoplankton and ecosystems.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What is acid rain?

options.A: Precipitation or deposition made more acidic mainly by sulphuric and nitric acids formed from sulphur dioxide and nitrogen oxides in the atmosphere
options.B: Rain made acidic by carbon dioxide only

questions.explanation: Acid rain is precipitation or deposition made more acidic mainly by sulphuric and nitric acids formed from sulphur dioxide and nitrogen oxides in the atmosphere.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What are major effects of acid rain?

options.A: Acidification of lakes and soils, damage to forests and aquatic life, nutrient leaching, mobilisation of toxic aluminium and corrosion of buildings and monuments
options.B: Only acidification of lakes

questions.explanation: Major effects of acid rain include acidification of lakes and soils, damage to forests and aquatic life, nutrient leaching, mobilisation of toxic aluminium and corrosion of buildings and monuments.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What is photochemical smog?

options.A: Air pollution formed when sunlight drives reactions involving nitrogen oxides and volatile organic compounds, producing ground-level ozone and other oxidants
options.B: Smoke from burning coal
options.D: Air pollution from sulphur dioxide only

questions.explanation: Photochemical smog is air pollution formed when sunlight drives reactions involving nitrogen oxides and volatile organic compounds, producing ground-level ozone and other oxidants.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What is El Niño?

options.A: The cool phase of ENSO
options.B: The warm phase of the El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO), involving unusually warm sea-surface temperatures in the central/eastern equatorial Pacific and changes in atmospheric circulation

questions.explanation: El Niño is the warm phase of the El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO), involving unusually warm sea-surface temperatures in the central/eastern equatorial Pacific and changes in atmospheric circulation.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What is La Niña?

options.A: The warm phase of ENSO
options.B: The cool phase of ENSO, involving unusually cool sea-surface temperatures in the central/eastern equatorial Pacific and associated atmospheric circulation changes

questions.explanation: La Niña is the cool phase of ENSO, involving unusually cool sea-surface temperatures in the central/eastern equatorial Pacific and associated atmospheric circulation changes.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: How can El Niño affect the Indian monsoon?

options.A: It guarantees drought every year
options.B: It is statistically associated with an increased likelihood of weaker Indian summer monsoon rainfall in many years, but the relationship is not deterministic and other climate drivers also matter
options.C: It has no effect on the Indian monsoon
options.D: It guarantees excess rainfall every year

questions.explanation: El Niño is statistically associated with an increased likelihood of weaker Indian summer monsoon rainfall in many years, but the relationship is not deterministic and other climate drivers also matter.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What is the Indian monsoon?

options.A: A seasonal reversal of winds associated with land-sea heating contrasts and large-scale atmospheric-oceanic circulation, bringing most of India's annual rainfall during the southwest monsoon season
options.B: A type of cyclone

questions.explanation: The Indian monsoon is a seasonal reversal of winds associated with land-sea heating contrasts and large-scale atmospheric-oceanic circulation, bringing most of India's annual rainfall during the southwest monsoon season.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What are extreme weather events?

options.A: Events such as heat waves, intense rainfall, droughts, floods and severe storms that are unusual or hazardous relative to local climate conditions
options.B: Only heat waves

questions.explanation: Extreme weather events are events such as heat waves, intense rainfall, droughts, floods and severe storms that are unusual or hazardous relative to local climate conditions.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What is a drought?

options.A: A prolonged period of abnormally low water availability relative to normal conditions, affecting rainfall, soil moisture, rivers, reservoirs or groundwater
options.B: A short period of heavy rainfall

questions.explanation: A drought is a prolonged period of abnormally low water availability relative to normal conditions, affecting rainfall, soil moisture, rivers, reservoirs or groundwater.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What is a flood?

options.A: Overflow or accumulation of water on land that is normally dry, caused by intense rainfall, river overflow, storm surge, dam failure or other factors
options.B: A prolonged period of low rainfall

questions.explanation: A flood is overflow or accumulation of water on land that is normally dry, caused by intense rainfall, river overflow, storm surge, dam failure or other factors.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What is a tropical cyclone?

options.A: A rotating, organised low-pressure storm system that forms over warm tropical or subtropical waters and has strong winds and heavy rainfall
options.B: A type of drought

questions.explanation: A tropical cyclone is a rotating, organised low-pressure storm system that forms over warm tropical or subtropical waters and has strong winds and heavy rainfall.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What is a heat wave?

options.A: A period of unusually hot weather relative to local conditions, often lasting several days and posing risks to health, agriculture and infrastructure; operational thresholds vary by region
options.B: A period of unusually cold weather

questions.explanation: A heat wave is a period of unusually hot weather relative to local conditions, often lasting several days and posing risks to health, agriculture and infrastructure; operational thresholds vary by region.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What is desertification?

options.A: The spread of existing deserts only
options.B: Land degradation in arid, semi-arid and dry sub-humid areas resulting from climatic variations and human activities; it is not simply the spread of existing deserts
options.C: The formation of new deserts only

questions.explanation: Desertification is land degradation in arid, semi-arid and dry sub-humid areas resulting from climatic variations and human activities; it is not simply the spread of existing deserts.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What causes sea-level rise?

options.A: Only melting glaciers
options.B: Primarily thermal expansion of warming seawater and addition of water from melting glaciers and ice sheets; local land movement also affects relative sea level

questions.explanation: Sea-level rise is primarily caused by thermal expansion of warming seawater and addition of water from melting glaciers and ice sheets; local land movement also affects relative sea level.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What is glacier retreat?

options.A: The growth of a glacier
options.B: The reduction in a glacier's mass and extent when ice loss exceeds accumulation over time, commonly associated with a warming climate
options.C: The formation of a new glacier

questions.explanation: Glacier retreat is the reduction in a glacier's mass and extent when ice loss exceeds accumulation over time, commonly associated with a warming climate.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What is climate adaptation?

options.A: Reducing greenhouse-gas emissions
options.B: Adjusting human or natural systems to actual or expected climate impacts to reduce harm or take advantage of beneficial opportunities

questions.explanation: Climate adaptation is adjusting human or natural systems to actual or expected climate impacts to reduce harm or take advantage of beneficial opportunities.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What is climate mitigation?

options.A: Adjusting to climate impacts
options.B: Reducing greenhouse-gas emissions or increasing greenhouse-gas removals, for example through clean energy, energy efficiency, forest protection and carbon capture

questions.explanation: Climate mitigation is reducing greenhouse-gas emissions or increasing greenhouse-gas removals, for example through clean energy, energy efficiency, forest protection and carbon capture.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What is sustainable development?

options.A: Development that meets present needs without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs, integrating economic, social and environmental dimensions
options.B: Development that ignores environmental concerns
options.C: Development that only focuses on economic growth
options.D: Development that only focuses on environmental protection

questions.explanation: Sustainable development is development that meets present needs without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs, integrating economic, social and environmental dimensions.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What is the Paris Agreement?

options.A: A legally binding international treaty adopted in 2015 under the UNFCCC, aiming to hold global temperature rise well below 2°C and pursue efforts to limit it to 1.5°C above pre-industrial levels
options.B: A treaty to phase out ozone-depleting substances

questions.explanation: The Paris Agreement is a legally binding international treaty adopted in 2015 under the UNFCCC, aiming to hold global temperature rise well below 2°C and pursue efforts to limit it to 1.5°C above pre-industrial levels.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What are Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs)?

options.A: Climate action plans submitted by Parties to the Paris Agreement, describing their mitigation and, where relevant, adaptation commitments; they are updated in successive cycles
options.B: A list of ozone-depleting substances

questions.explanation: NDCs are climate action plans submitted by Parties to the Paris Agreement, describing their mitigation and, where relevant, adaptation commitments; they are updated in successive cycles.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What was the Kyoto Protocol?

options.A: A 1997 protocol to the UNFCCC that established legally binding greenhouse-gas emission reduction targets for many developed countries for commitment periods
options.B: A 1987 treaty to phase out ozone-depleting substances

questions.explanation: The Kyoto Protocol was a 1997 protocol to the UNFCCC that established legally binding greenhouse-gas emission reduction targets for many developed countries for commitment periods.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What is the Montreal Protocol?

options.A: A 1987 international treaty to protect the ozone layer by phasing out production and consumption of ozone-depleting substances; it has achieved near-universal ratification
options.B: A 1997 protocol on greenhouse-gas emissions

questions.explanation: The Montreal Protocol is a 1987 international treaty to protect the ozone layer by phasing out production and consumption of ozone-depleting substances; it has achieved near-universal ratification.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What is the Kigali Amendment?

options.A: A 2016 amendment to the Montreal Protocol that provides for the phasedown of hydrofluorocarbons (HFCs), potent greenhouse gases that do not deplete ozone
options.B: A 1997 protocol on greenhouse-gas emissions

questions.explanation: The Kigali Amendment is a 2016 amendment to the Montreal Protocol that provides for the phasedown of hydrofluorocarbons (HFCs), potent greenhouse gases that do not deplete ozone.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What is the UNFCCC?

options.A: The United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change, adopted in 1992, the main international framework for cooperation on climate change
options.B: A treaty on biological diversity

questions.explanation: The UNFCCC is the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change, adopted in 1992, the main international framework for cooperation on climate change.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What is the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD)?

options.A: A 1992 international treaty with three objectives: conservation of biodiversity, sustainable use of its components and fair and equitable sharing of benefits from genetic resources
options.B: A treaty on climate change

questions.explanation: The CBD is a 1992 international treaty with three objectives: conservation of biodiversity, sustainable use of its components and fair and equitable sharing of benefits from genetic resources.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What is CITES?

options.A: The Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora, which regulates international trade in listed wild animals and plants to ensure trade does not threaten their survival
options.B: A treaty on climate change

questions.explanation: CITES is the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora, which regulates international trade in listed wild animals and plants to ensure trade does not threaten their survival.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What is the Ramsar Convention?

options.A: An international treaty adopted in 1971 for the conservation and wise use of wetlands; it is named after Ramsar, Iran
options.B: A treaty on climate change

questions.explanation: The Ramsar Convention is an international treaty adopted in 1971 for the conservation and wise use of wetlands; it is named after Ramsar, Iran.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What is the UN Convention to Combat Desertification (UNCCD)?

options.A: A 1994 international agreement addressing desertification, land degradation and drought, particularly in drylands
options.B: A treaty on climate change

questions.explanation: The UNCCD is a 1994 international agreement addressing desertification, land degradation and drought, particularly in drylands.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What is the Basel Convention?

options.A: A treaty controlling transboundary movements of hazardous wastes and their disposal, aiming to protect human health and the environment
options.B: A treaty on climate change

questions.explanation: The Basel Convention is a treaty controlling transboundary movements of hazardous wastes and their disposal, aiming to protect human health and the environment.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What is the Stockholm Convention?

options.A: A treaty adopted in 2001 to protect human health and the environment from persistent organic pollutants (POPs)
options.B: A treaty on climate change

questions.explanation: The Stockholm Convention is a treaty adopted in 2001 to protect human health and the environment from persistent organic pollutants (POPs).

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What is the Minamata Convention?

options.A: A global treaty adopted in 2013 to protect human health and the environment from anthropogenic emissions and releases of mercury
options.B: A treaty on climate change

questions.explanation: The Minamata Convention is a global treaty adopted in 2013 to protect human health and the environment from anthropogenic emissions and releases of mercury.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What is the Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction?

options.A: A 2015-2030 global framework to prevent new disaster risk and reduce existing risk through understanding risk, strengthening governance, investing in resilience and improving preparedness
options.B: A treaty on climate change

questions.explanation: The Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction is a 2015-2030 global framework to prevent new disaster risk and reduce existing risk through understanding risk, strengthening governance, investing in resilience and improving preparedness.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What is the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986?

options.A: An umbrella Indian law enacted to protect and improve the environment and prevent hazards to humans, other living creatures, plants and property; it empowers the Central Government to take measures and set rules/standards
options.B: A law to prevent water pollution only
options.C: A law to prevent air pollution only
options.D: A law to protect wildlife only

questions.explanation: The Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 is an umbrella Indian law enacted to protect and improve the environment and prevent hazards to humans, other living creatures, plants and property; it empowers the Central Government to take measures and set rules/standards.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: Why was the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 enacted?

options.A: It followed the 1972 Stockholm Conference and was enacted in the context of the Bhopal gas disaster and the need for comprehensive environmental protection legislation
options.B: It followed the 1992 Rio Conference

options.B: Afforestation

questions.explanation: Common causes of soil pollution include excessive pesticides and fertilisers, industrial waste, mining, oil spills, landfill leakage, sewage sludge contamination and improper disposal of hazardous waste.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: Which of the following is an effect of prolonged noise exposure?

options.A: Hearing loss
options.B: Improved concentration

questions.explanation: Effects of prolonged noise exposure include hearing loss, sleep disturbance, stress, impaired concentration and cardiovascular effects; wildlife communication and behaviour can also be disrupted.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: Which of the following is a stage of sewage treatment?

options.A: Primary settling
options.B: Deforestation

questions.explanation: The usual stages of sewage treatment are preliminary treatment (screens and grit removal), primary settling, secondary biological treatment and, where needed, tertiary/advanced treatment and disinfection.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: Which of the following is a type of solid waste?

options.A: Biomedical waste
options.B: Wastewater

questions.explanation: Solid waste management includes segregation, collection, storage, transport, processing, recovery and safe disposal of solid waste; biomedical waste is a type of solid waste.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: Which of the following is a preferred option in the waste hierarchy?

options.A: Prevention/reduction
options.B: Disposal

questions.explanation: The waste hierarchy is a preferred order of waste management: prevention/reduction, preparing for reuse, recycling, recovery and, as a last resort, disposal.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: Which of the following is a source segregation stream?

options.A: Wet/biodegradable waste
options.B: Wastewater

questions.explanation: Source segregation of waste is separating waste where it is generated into appropriate streams, such as wet/biodegradable, dry/recyclable and domestic hazardous or sanitary waste, according to local rules.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: Which of the following is a major greenhouse gas?

options.A: Carbon dioxide
options.B: Oxygen

questions.explanation: Major greenhouse gases include water vapour, carbon dioxide, methane, nitrous oxide, ozone and fluorinated gases.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: Which of the following is a cause of ozone-layer depletion?

options.A: CFCs and halons
options.B: Carbon dioxide

questions.explanation: Ozone-depleting substances such as CFCs and halons release chlorine or bromine in the stratosphere, catalytically destroying ozone.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: Which of the following is an effect of ozone depletion?

options.A: Increased risk of skin cancer
options.B: Decreased UV radiation

questions.explanation: Effects of ozone depletion include more harmful UV-B reaching Earth's surface, increasing risks of skin cancer, cataracts and immune effects and harming crops, phytoplankton and ecosystems.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: Which of the following is a major effect of acid rain?

options.A: Acidification of lakes and soils
options.B: Increased soil fertility

questions.explanation: Major effects of acid rain include acidification of lakes and soils, damage to forests and aquatic life, nutrient leaching, mobilisation of toxic aluminium and corrosion of buildings and monuments.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: Which of the following is a component of photochemical smog?

options.A: Ground-level ozone
options.B: Stratospheric ozone

questions.explanation: Photochemical smog is air pollution formed when sunlight drives reactions involving nitrogen oxides and volatile organic compounds, producing ground-level ozone and other oxidants.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: Which of the following is an extreme weather event?

options.A: Heat wave
options.B: Gentle breeze

questions.explanation: Extreme weather events include heat waves, intense rainfall, droughts, floods and severe storms that are unusual or hazardous relative to local climate conditions.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: Which of the following is a cause of sea-level rise?

options.A: Thermal expansion of warming seawater
options.B: Decreased melting of glaciers

questions.explanation: Sea-level rise is primarily caused by thermal expansion of warming seawater and addition of water from melting glaciers and ice sheets; local land movement also affects relative sea level.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: Which of the following is a climate mitigation measure?

options.A: Clean energy
options.B: Building sea walls

questions.explanation: Climate mitigation is reducing greenhouse-gas emissions or increasing greenhouse-gas removals, for example through clean energy, energy efficiency, forest protection and carbon capture.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: Which of the following is a climate adaptation measure?

options.A: Building sea walls
options.B: Switching to solar energy

questions.explanation: Climate adaptation is adjusting human or natural systems to actual or expected climate impacts to reduce harm or take advantage of beneficial opportunities; building sea walls is an example.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: Which treaty aims to hold global temperature rise well below 2°C and pursue efforts to limit it to 1.5°C?

options.A: Paris Agreement
options.B: Kyoto Protocol

questions.explanation: The Paris Agreement aims to hold global temperature rise well below 2°C and pursue efforts to limit it to 1.5°C above pre-industrial levels.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: Which treaty established legally binding greenhouse-gas emission reduction targets for many developed countries?

options.A: Kyoto Protocol
options.B: Paris Agreement

questions.explanation: The Kyoto Protocol was a 1997 protocol to the UNFCCC that established legally binding greenhouse-gas emission reduction targets for many developed countries for commitment periods.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: Which treaty has three objectives: conservation of biodiversity, sustainable use of its components and fair and equitable sharing of benefits from genetic resources?

options.A: CBD
options.B: CITES

questions.explanation: The Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD) is a 1992 international treaty with three objectives: conservation of biodiversity, sustainable use of its components and fair and equitable sharing of benefits from genetic resources.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: Which treaty regulates international trade in listed wild animals and plants?

options.A: CITES
options.B: CBD

questions.explanation: CITES is the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora, which regulates international trade in listed wild animals and plants to ensure trade does not threaten their survival.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: Which treaty addresses desertification, land degradation and drought?

options.A: UNCCD
options.B: CBD

questions.explanation: The UNCCD is a 1994 international agreement addressing desertification, land degradation and drought, particularly in drylands.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: Which treaty controls transboundary movements of hazardous wastes and their disposal?

options.A: Basel Convention
options.B: Stockholm Convention

questions.explanation: The Basel Convention is a treaty controlling transboundary movements of hazardous wastes and their disposal, aiming to protect human health and the environment.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: Which treaty protects human health and the environment from persistent organic pollutants (POPs)?

options.A: Stockholm Convention
options.B: Basel Convention

questions.explanation: The Stockholm Convention is a treaty adopted in 2001 to protect human health and the environment from persistent organic pollutants (POPs).

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: Which treaty protects human health and the environment from anthropogenic emissions and releases of mercury?

options.A: Minamata Convention
options.B: Basel Convention

questions.explanation: The Minamata Convention is a global treaty adopted in 2013 to protect human health and the environment from anthropogenic emissions and releases of mercury.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: Which Indian law is an umbrella law for environmental protection?

options.A: Environment (Protection) Act, 1986
options.B: Water Act, 1974

questions.explanation: The Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 is an umbrella Indian law enacted to protect and improve the environment and prevent hazards to humans, other living creatures, plants and property.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: Which Indian law provides for pollution control boards and regulatory powers for water pollution?

options.A: Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974
options.B: Air Act, 1981

questions.explanation: The Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974 provides for pollution control boards and regulatory powers for water pollution.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: Which Indian law provides for pollution control boards and regulatory functions for air pollution?

options.A: Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1981
options.B: Water Act, 1974

questions.explanation: The Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1981 provides for relevant pollution control boards and regulatory functions for air pollution.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: Which Indian law deals with conservation of biological diversity, sustainable use of its components and fair and equitable sharing of benefits?

options.A: Biological Diversity Act, 2002
options.B: Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972

questions.explanation: The Biological Diversity Act, 2002 is an Indian law for conservation of biological diversity, sustainable use of its components and fair and equitable sharing of benefits arising from use of biological resources and associated knowledge.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: Under which Act was the National Green Tribunal established?

options.A: National Green Tribunal Act, 2010
options.B: Environment (Protection) Act, 1986

questions.explanation: The National Green Tribunal (NGT) is a specialised Indian tribunal established under the National Green Tribunal Act, 2010.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: Under which Act was the Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) constituted?

options.A: Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974
options.B: Air Act, 1981

questions.explanation: The CPCB is a statutory organisation constituted under the Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: Under which Act was the National Tiger Conservation Authority (NTCA) constituted?

options.A: Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972, as amended in 2006
options.B: Environment (Protection) Act, 1986

questions.explanation: The NTCA is a statutory body constituted under the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972, as amended in 2006, to strengthen tiger conservation and oversee related measures.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: Which ministry formulates environmental and forest policies at the Union level in India?

options.A: MoEFCC
options.B: Ministry of Agriculture

questions.explanation: The Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change (MoEFCC) formulates environmental and forest policies, administers major environmental laws, supports conservation, addresses climate change, and coordinates with national and international institutions.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: Which notification is central to the current EIA regulatory framework in India?

options.A: EIA Notification, 2006
options.B: EIA Notification, 1991

questions.explanation: The EIA Notification, 2006 issued under the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986, as amended from time to time, is central to the current EIA regulatory framework.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: How many national missions were originally under India's NAPCC?

options.A: Eight
options.B: Five

questions.explanation: The original eight national missions under India's NAPCC are National Solar Mission; Enhanced Energy Efficiency; Sustainable Habitat; Water; Sustaining the Himalayan Ecosystem; Green India; Sustainable Agriculture; and Strategic Knowledge for Climate Change.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: Which of the following is one of the original eight national missions under India's NAPCC?

options.A: National Solar Mission
options.B: National Wind Mission

questions.explanation: The National Solar Mission is one of the original eight national missions under India's NAPCC.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: Which of the following is one of the original eight national missions under India's NAPCC?

options.A: Green India
options.B: Blue India

questions.explanation: Green India is one of the original eight national missions under India's NAPCC.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: Which of the following is one of the original eight national missions under India's NAPCC?

options.A: Sustainable Agriculture
options.B: Sustainable Fisheries

questions.explanation: Sustainable Agriculture is one of the original eight national missions under India's NAPCC.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: Which of the following is one of the original eight national missions under India's NAPCC?

options.A: Sustaining the Himalayan Ecosystem
options.B: Sustaining the Western Ghats

questions.explanation: Sustaining the Himalayan Ecosystem is one of the original eight national missions under India's NAPCC.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: Which of the following is one of the original eight national missions under India's NAPCC?

options.A: Strategic Knowledge for Climate Change
options.B: Strategic Knowledge for Biodiversity

questions.explanation: Strategic Knowledge for Climate Change is one of the original eight national missions under India's NAPCC.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: Which of the following is one of the original eight national missions under India's NAPCC?

options.A: Enhanced Energy Efficiency
options.B: Enhanced Water Efficiency

questions.explanation: Enhanced Energy Efficiency is one of the original eight national missions under India's NAPCC.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: Which of the following is one of the original eight national missions under India's NAPCC?

options.A: Sustainable Habitat
options.B: Sustainable Transport

questions.explanation: Sustainable Habitat is one of the original eight national missions under India's NAPCC.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: Which of the following is one of the original eight national missions under India's NAPCC?

options.A: Water
options.B: Air

questions.explanation: Water is one of the original eight national missions under India's NAPCC.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: Which programme was launched in 2014 to reduce pollution and rejuvenate the River Ganga?

options.A: Namami Gange
options.B: Project Tiger

questions.explanation: Namami Gange is an integrated conservation programme launched in 2014 to reduce pollution and rejuvenate the River Ganga through sewage treatment, river-surface cleaning, biodiversity, afforestation and public participation measures.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: Which India-led initiative launched in 2022 encourages individual and community actions for environmentally sustainable lifestyles?

options.A: Mission LIFE
options.B: Swachh Bharat Mission

questions.explanation: Mission LIFE is Mission Lifestyle for Environment, an India-led initiative launched in 2022 that encourages individual and community actions for environmentally sustainable lifestyles and resource-efficient behaviour.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: Which principle states that lack of full scientific certainty should not be used as a reason to postpone cost-effective preventive measures where there is a threat of serious or irreversible environmental harm?

options.A: Precautionary principle
options.B: Polluter pays principle

questions.explanation: The precautionary principle states that where there is a threat of serious or irreversible environmental harm, lack of full scientific certainty should not be used as a reason to postpone cost-effective preventive measures.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: Which principle states that the polluter should bear the costs of preventing, controlling and remedying pollution?

options.A: Polluter pays principle
options.B: Precautionary principle

questions.explanation: The polluter pays principle states that the polluter should bear the costs of preventing, controlling and remedying pollution, including appropriate compensation and restoration costs.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: Which principle states that certain natural resources are held by the state in trust for public use and cannot be treated as unrestricted private property?

options.A: Public trust doctrine
options.B: Precautionary principle

questions.explanation: The public trust doctrine is the principle that certain natural resources are held by the state in trust for public use and cannot be treated as unrestricted private property.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: Which Article directs the State to protect and improve the environment and safeguard forests and wildlife?

options.A: Article 48A
options.B: Article 51A(g)

questions.explanation: Article 48A directs the State to protect and improve the environment and safeguard forests and wildlife.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: Which Article makes it a fundamental duty of citizens to protect and improve the natural environment?

options.A: Article 51A(g)
options.B: Article 48A

questions.explanation: Article 51A(g) makes it a fundamental duty of citizens to protect and improve the natural environment.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: Which Article has been interpreted by Indian courts to include aspects of a clean and healthy environment?

options.A: Article 21
options.B: Article 14

questions.explanation: Article 21, the right to life, has been interpreted by Indian courts to include aspects of a clean and healthy environment.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: What is required for specified projects under applicable environmental regulations after the prescribed appraisal and decision process?

options.A: Environmental clearance
options.B: Pollution tax

questions.explanation: An environmental clearance is a formal approval required for specified projects under applicable environmental regulations after the prescribed appraisal and decision process; conditions and monitoring obligations may apply.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: Which of the following is a role of local bodies in environmental protection?

options.A: Solid-waste management
options.B: Formulating national environmental policy

questions.explanation: Local bodies support sanitation, solid-waste management, drainage, local water conservation, public awareness and implementation of relevant municipal and environmental rules.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: Which of the following statements about the 10 percent law of energy transfer is correct?

options.A: It was proposed by Raymond Lindeman and states that, on average, only about 10% of energy at one trophic level is transferred to the next
options.B: It was proposed by Ernst Haeckel and states that 10% of energy is recycled
options.C: It states that 10% of energy is lost at each trophic level
options.D: It states that 10% of energy is transferred from consumers to producers

questions.explanation: Raymond Lindeman's ecological generalisation states that, on average, only about 10% of energy at one trophic level is transferred to the next; the actual proportion varies.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: Which of the following is an example of an inverted pyramid of numbers?

options.A: One tree supporting many insects and parasites
options.B: Many grasses supporting few herbivores

questions.explanation: Yes. For example, one tree may support many insects and parasites, producing an inverted or irregular pyramid of numbers.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: Which of the following is an example of an inverted pyramid of biomass?

options.A: In some aquatic ecosystems, the standing biomass of phytoplankton is lower than that of zooplankton at a given moment
options.B: In a forest, the biomass of trees is lower than that of herbivores
options.C: In a grassland, the biomass of grasses is lower than that of herbivores
options.D: In a desert, the biomass of producers is lower than that of consumers

questions.explanation: Yes. In some aquatic ecosystems, the standing biomass of phytoplankton is lower than that of zooplankton at a given moment because phytoplankton reproduce and turn over rapidly.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: Which of the following statements about ecological balance is correct?

options.A: It is a dynamic condition in which interactions and natural processes maintain ecosystem functions and populations within changing limits; it does not mean that nature is static
options.B: It is a static condition where nothing changes

questions.explanation: Ecological balance is a dynamic condition in which interactions and natural processes maintain ecosystem functions and populations within changing limits; it does not mean that nature is static.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: Which of the following statements about climax communities is correct?

options.A: A climax community is a traditional term for a relatively stable late-successional community under a given set of conditions; modern ecology recognises that communities may remain dynamic and need not reach one fixed climax
options.B: A climax community is the first community to colonise bare rock
options.D: A climax community consists only of pioneer species

questions.explanation: A climax community is a traditional term for a relatively stable late-successional community under a given set of conditions; modern ecology recognises that communities may remain dynamic and need not reach one fixed climax.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: Which of the following statements about carrying capacity is correct?

options.A: It is the maximum population size an environment can sustain over time under prevailing resource and environmental conditions; it can change when conditions change
options.B: It is the minimum population size for survival
options.C: It is the total number of species in an area
options.D: It is the rate of energy transfer between trophic levels

questions.explanation: Carrying capacity is the maximum population size an environment can sustain over time under prevailing resource and environmental conditions; it can change when conditions change.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: Which of the following statements about renewable resources is correct?

options.A: Renewable resources can be depleted or degraded if extraction exceeds their rate of renewal or if ecosystems are damaged
options.B: Renewable resources are always inexhaustible
options.C: Renewable resources form much more slowly than they are consumed
options.D: Renewable resources cannot be used by humans

questions.explanation: No. Renewable resources can be depleted or degraded if extraction exceeds their rate of renewal or if ecosystems are damaged.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: Which of the following statements about sustainable utilisation is correct?

options.A: Using resources at rates and in ways that maintain ecological integrity and do not undermine the ability of future generations to meet their needs
options.B: Using resources as fast as possible
options.C: Not using any resources at all

questions.explanation: Sustainable utilisation is using resources at rates and in ways that maintain ecological integrity and do not undermine the ability of future generations to meet their needs.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: Which of the following statements about Data Deficient species is correct?

options.A: Data Deficient means available information is insufficient to assess extinction risk; it does not mean low risk
options.B: Data Deficient means the species is safe
options.C: Data Deficient means the species is extinct
options.D: Data Deficient means the species is invasive

questions.explanation: No. Data Deficient means available information is insufficient to assess extinction risk; it does not mean low risk.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: Which of the following statements about invasive alien species is correct?

options.A: An alien species occurs outside its natural range due to human activity or other introduction; it is termed invasive when it spreads and causes or is likely to cause harm
options.B: Alien and invasive are the same thing
options.C: An alien species is always harmful
options.D: An invasive species is always native

questions.explanation: An alien species occurs outside its natural range due to human activity or other introduction; it is termed invasive when it spreads and causes or is likely to cause harm.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: Which of the following statements about the difference between a national park, sanctuary and biosphere reserve is correct?

options.A: A national park and sanctuary are statutory protected-area categories under Indian wildlife law; a biosphere reserve is a landscape-level designation under the UNESCO MAB framework and may include protected areas and inhabited sustainable-use zones
options.B: They are all the same
options.C: A biosphere reserve is a statutory category under Indian wildlife law
options.D: A national park is a UNESCO designation

questions.explanation: A national park and sanctuary are statutory protected-area categories under Indian wildlife law; a biosphere reserve is a landscape-level designation under the UNESCO MAB framework and may include protected areas and inhabited sustainable-use zones.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: Which of the following statements about BOD and COD is correct?

options.A: BOD measures oxygen used by microorganisms to break down biodegradable organic matter; COD measures the oxygen equivalent required to chemically oxidise substances in water
options.B: BOD measures chemical oxidation; COD measures biological oxidation
options.C: BOD and COD are the same
options.D: BOD measures oxygen produced by photosynthesis; COD measures oxygen used by microorganisms

questions.explanation: BOD is the amount of dissolved oxygen used by microorganisms to break down biodegradable organic matter in a water sample under specified test conditions; COD is an analytical measure of the oxygen equivalent required to chemically oxidise substances in water.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: Which of the following statements about eutrophication is correct?

options.A: Eutrophication is excess nutrient enrichment of water, often by nitrogen and phosphorus, causing excessive algal or plant growth and sometimes oxygen depletion and fish kills
options.B: Eutrophication is depletion of nutrients in water
options.C: Eutrophication is increase in oxygen levels in water
options.D: Eutrophication is decrease in water temperature

questions.explanation: Eutrophication is excess nutrient enrichment of water, often by nitrogen and phosphorus, causing excessive algal or plant growth and sometimes oxygen depletion and fish kills.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: Which of the following statements about biodegradable waste is correct?

options.A: Poorly managed biodegradable waste can generate methane, leachate, odours and pathogens; management conditions matter
options.B: Biodegradable waste is always harmless

questions.explanation: No. Poorly managed biodegradable waste can generate methane, leachate, odours and pathogens; management conditions matter.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: Which of the following statements about leachate is correct?

options.A: Leachate is liquid that has percolated through waste and carries dissolved or suspended contaminants; it must be collected and treated at engineered landfills
options.B: Leachate is a type of gas from landfills
options.C: Leachate is a type of compost
options.D: Leachate is a type of plastic

questions.explanation: Leachate is liquid that has percolated through waste and carries dissolved or suspended contaminants; it must be collected and treated at engineered landfills.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: Which of the following statements about the natural and enhanced greenhouse effect is correct?

options.A: The natural greenhouse effect supports life; the enhanced greenhouse effect from human emissions drives modern global warming
options.B: The natural greenhouse effect is harmful; the enhanced greenhouse effect is beneficial

questions.explanation: The natural greenhouse effect supports life; the enhanced greenhouse effect from human emissions drives modern global warming.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: Which of the following statements about acid rain is correct?

options.A: Acid rain is mainly linked to sulphur dioxide and nitrogen oxides, not carbon dioxide alone
options.B: Acid rain is mainly linked to carbon dioxide alone
options.C: Acid rain is mainly linked to methane and ozone
options.D: Acid rain is mainly linked to CFCs and halons

questions.explanation: Acid rain is mainly linked to sulphur dioxide and nitrogen oxides, not carbon dioxide alone.

questions.subject: Environmental Science & Ecology
questions.question: Which of the following statements about ground-level ozone and stratospheric ozone is correct?
